orig_9709_p3_alg_modulus_graphs.description: Interpret modulus as distance and sketch the graph of the modulus of a linear expression for Cambridge 9709 Pure 3.

sections.title: What does a modulus measure?
sections.label: Read modulus as distance
sections.intro: \(|u|\) is the distance from \(u\) to \(0\) on a number line. It is always non-negative and is zero exactly when \(u=0\).

blocks.html:
\[|u|=\begin{cases}u,&u\geqslant0,\\-u,&u<0.\end{cases}\]

Apply the rule to the value inside the bars. For instance, when \(x=-2\), \(x-1=-3\) and \(|x-1|=3\).

blocks.title: Evaluate both inputs
blocks.hint: Find the signed value inside the bars at each input first.

retry.feedback: The inner expression is negative, so take its opposite.

blocks.html: A distance from \(r\) has the form \(|x-r|\). If a positive number multiplies the input difference, it scales the height by that number.

blocks.title: Read the centre of a distance model
blocks.hint: Factor two from the inner expression and rewrite the remaining linear expression as x minus the centre.

sections.title: How do I sketch the two lines?
sections.label: Sketch vertex and gradients
sections.intro: Start with the line \(y=ax+b\). Keep its points on or above the \(x\)-axis. A point below it has negative height, so reflect that part upwards. Both parts keep the same \(x\)-coordinates. They join at \((x,0)\), where \(ax+b=0\).

blocks.html:
\[y=|a|\left|x+\frac{b}{a}\right|.\]

The minimum is \(0\), at \(x=-\frac ba\). To its left the gradient is \(-|a|\), and to its right the gradient is \(|a|\). The \(y\)-intercept is \((0,|b|)\).

figure.alt: A V-shaped graph of y equals the modulus of 2x minus 6. The vertex is at (3, 0), the y-intercept is (0, 6), and the two branches have gradients −2 and 2.
figure.caption: The vertex is \( (3,0) \). The two branches have gradients \( -2 \) and \( 2 \).

blocks.html: When \(a<0\), the inside expression is positive to the left of the vertex. The graph still falls as you approach the vertex from the left.

blocks.title: Find the key features of a sketch
blocks.prompt: For \(y=|-4x+2|\), give the vertex's \(x\)-coordinate, the \(y\)-intercept's \(y\)-coordinate and both gradients.
blocks.hint: Solve \(-4x+2=0\). Use the magnitude of \(-4\) as the size of both gradients.
blocks.solution: The vertex is \(\left(\frac12,0\right)\), the \(y\)-intercept is \((0,2)\), and the left and right gradients are \(-4\) and \(4\).

blocks.html: The size of the slope of the inner line decides how steep the V is. Both arms have slope of size \(|a|\). The left arm decreases to the vertex and the right arm increases from it.

blocks.title: Find both arms of a negatively written V
blocks.prompt: For \(y=|-3x+12|\), give the vertex's x-coordinate, the y-intercept value and the gradients of the left and right arms.
blocks.hint: Rewrite as three times a non-negative distance and decide which branch decreases towards the vertex.
blocks.solution: \(y=3|x-4|\) has vertex \((4,0)\) and intercept \((0,12)\). The left and right gradients are \(-3\) and \(3\) respectively.

sections.title: How many times does a horizontal line meet the graph?
sections.label: Read horizontal intersections
sections.intro: Compare the requested height with the minimum \(0\). A negative height cannot occur, height zero meets the graph at the vertex, and a positive height meets both arms when \(a\ne0\).

blocks.title: Find both intersections
blocks.hint: Starting at \(x=-2\), move \(\frac93=3\) units in each direction.
blocks.solution: Solve \(3x+6=9\) or \(3x+6=-9\). The answers are \(x=1\) and \(x=-5\).

retry.feedback: The line also crosses the left branch.
The line also crosses the right branch.

blocks.html: Label the axes, vertex and intercepts. A sketch illustrates the algebraic values you have found.
At a fixed positive height the two inputs are mirror images in the vertical line through the vertex. If the distance from the vertex is \(d\), write the inputs as \(r-d\) and \(r+d\).

blocks.title: Find every input at a given height
blocks.prompt: Find all inputs where \(y=|4x+12|\) meets the line \(y=20\).
blocks.hint: Rewrite the graph as four times a distance from the vertex.
blocks.solution: The vertex is at \(x=-3\) and the distance from it is \(5\). Thus \(x=-8\) or \(x=2\).

sections.title: How do I read a formula from the vertex and another point?
sections.label: Recover a V from two points
sections.intro: For a V with vertex \((r,0)\) and another point \((p,h)\), the height \(h\) tells you how many times the distance from the vertex was scaled.

blocks.html: When \(p\ne r\) and \(h>0\), use \(y=k|x-r|\) with \(k=\frac{h}{|p-r|}\). To write \(y=|ax+b|\), one choice is \(a=k\) and \(b=-kr\).

blocks.title: Find a and b from two graph points
blocks.prompt: The graph \(y=|ax+b|\) has vertex \((3,0)\) and contains \((-1,8)\). Find \(a,b\) with \(a>0\).
blocks.hint: Use the distance between −1 and 3 to find the positive scale.
blocks.solution: The distance is four, giving \(a=2\). The formula is \(y=2|x-3|=|2x-6|\), so \(b=-6\).

examples.title: Same height, different inputs
examples.question: Evaluate \(|x-2|\) at \(x=-1\) and \(x=5\).
solution: At \(x=-1\), the expression inside the bars is \(-1-2=-3\). Its distance from zero is \(3\).
At \(x=5\), the inside value is \(5-2=3\). Its modulus is also \(3\).
The two inputs lie \(3\) units to either side of \(x=2\).

examples.title: Sketch a shifted V
examples.question: Sketch \(y=|2x-6|\), labelling the vertex, intercepts and gradients.
solution: Solve \(2x-6=0\). The vertex is \((3,0)\) and is the only \(x\)-intercept.
At \(x=0\), \(y=|-6|=6\), so the graph meets the \(y\)-axis at \((0,6)\).
To the left of \(3\), the line \(y=2x-6\) has negative height. Reflect it in the \(x\)-axis to get \(y=-2x+6\). To the right, keep \(y=2x-6\). Their gradients are \(-2\) and \(2\).

examples.title: Find two points at a prescribed height
examples.question: Where does the line \(y=4\) meet \(y=|2x-6|\)?
solution: Rewrite the height condition as \(2|x-3|=4\), so \(|x-3|=2\).
Move \(2\) units to either side of \(3\), giving \(x=1\) or \(x=5\).
The intersections are \((1,4)\) and \((5,4)\).

examples.title: Read a scaled distance
examples.question: Interpret the height of the graph \(y=|3x-6|\) at \(x=-1\). Find the point on the other arm at the same height.
solution: Rewrite the formula as \(y=3|x-2|\). The height is three times the horizontal distance from \(x=2\).
At \(x=-1\) that distance is three. The height is \(9\) and the other input is \(x=2+3=5\).

examples.title: Sketch a V when the inner slope is negative
examples.question: Give the vertex, the vertical intercept and both branch gradients of \(y=|-5x-10|\).
solution: The inner line vanishes at \(x=-2\), so the vertex is \((-2,0)\).
Since \(y=5|x+2|\), the left arm has gradient \(-5\) and the right arm has gradient \(5\).
At \(x=0\) the modulus is \(10\), giving the intercept \((0,10)\).

examples.title: Recover the second intersection by symmetry
examples.question: The line \(y=8\) meets \(y=|2x-10|\) at an input \(x=9\). Find the other input.
solution: The vertex has input \(5\). The known input is four units to its right.
The other input is four units to its left, \(x=1\). Both have height \(2\times4=8\).

examples.title: Build a formula from a given vertex
examples.question: A graph of the form \(y=|ax+b|\) has vertex \((-2,0)\) and passes through \((4,18)\). Find one formula with \(a>0\).
solution: The form is \(y=k|x+2|\). The extra point is six horizontal units from the vertex.

glossary.definition: Distance from zero on the real number line.
The corner of the V, where the inside expression is zero.
The signed change in height per unit increase in the input.
The vertical line through the vertex. Points on the two arms at the same height are equally far from this line.
A positive multiplier that converts horizontal distance from the vertex into graph height.
A point that lies on both graphs. Its x-coordinate is a solution to the equation made by equating the graph heights.

revision.body:
Distance and the two branches

\(|u|=u\) for \(u\ge0\) and \(|u|=-u\) for \(u<0\). For \(a\ne0\), \(y=|ax+b|\) has vertex \(\left(-\frac ba,0\right)\), \(y\)-intercept \((0,|b|)\) and gradients \(-|a|\), then \(|a|\).

Sketch example

\(y=|2x-6|=2|x-3|\) has vertex \((3,0)\) and passes through \((0,6)\).

Read a horizontal intersection

If \(c>0\), \(|ax+b|=c\) gives two points at distance \(\frac{c}{|a|}\) from the vertex. At \(c=0\) there is one point, and at \(c<0\) there are none.

Recover the scale

A point \((p,h)\) on a V with vertex \((r,0)\) gives \(k=\frac{h}{|p-r|}\) for \(y=k|x-r|\).
revision.checks:
• Find the vertex at the zero of the inside expression.
  • Leave the positive part of the original line in place.
  • Reflect its negative part in the \(x\)-axis.
revision.examTip: If \(a<0\), the formula for the left arm changes, but its gradient is still \(-|a|\).

extraPractice.title: Factor out the positive scale
extraPractice.hint: Inside the modulus factor out negative two.

extraPractice.title: Find the contact with the horizontal axis
extraPractice.hint: The only number with zero modulus is zero.

extraPractice.title: Decide whether the V meets a negative height
extraPractice.hint: Check the possible heights of the V.
extraPractice.solution: Every height of the V is non-negative, so the graphs have no intersection.

extraPractice.title: Find the two exact intersections
extraPractice.hint: The vertex is at two thirds. Find the distance from the vertex for height four.

orig_9709_p3_alg_modulus_equations.description: Find complete solution sets for modulus equations using signed cases and test every candidate in the original equation.

sections.title: How do I solve a modulus equal to a constant?
sections.label: Use both signed cases
sections.intro: For \(|u|=c\), decide how many solutions are possible by checking the sign of \(c\) before splitting into cases.

blocks.html: If \(c>0\), use \(u=c\) or \(u=-c\). If \(c=0\), use \(u=0\) once. If \(c<0\), the solution set is empty.

Choose a route by looking at the other side. With a fixed height, check its sign. With a second modulus, compare equal and opposite insides. With a signed expression, restrict it to non-negative values before solving.

blocks.title: Find the full root set
blocks.hint: The inside value can be \(8\) or \(-8\).

retry.feedback: Also solve the case where the inside value is negative.
Also solve the case where the inside value is positive.

blocks.html: When the target height is zero the two signed cases coincide. Give the one input that makes the inside expression zero.

blocks.title: Use the zero-height case
blocks.hint: Solve the inner expression equal to zero.
blocks.solution: Solving \(6x-5=0\) gives the single solution \(x=\frac56\).

sections.title: What changes when both sides contain a modulus?
sections.label: Compare two moduli
sections.intro: Equal distances from zero mean that the two signed expressions are equal or opposite.

blocks.html:
\[|u|=|v|\iff u=v\ \text{or}\ u=-v.\]

You can also square both sides because both moduli are non-negative, then factor \(u^2-v^2=(u-v)(u+v)\). This is an equivalence.

blocks.title: Keep every solution
blocks.hint: Use \(2x+5=x-4\) and \(2x+5=-(x-4)\) as separate equations.
blocks.solution: The first gives \(x=-9\). The second gives \(3x=-1\), so \(x=-\frac13\).

blocks.html: When the whole expression changes sign, every term inside its brackets changes sign.
One signed equation may have no solution because its variable terms cancel and leave a false constant equality. Complete the other case as well.

blocks.title: Solve when one case is impossible
blocks.hint: Equal inner expressions would give −1 = 7. Test the opposite-sign equation.
blocks.solution: The only possible case is \(4x-1=-4x-7\), giving \(8x=-6\) and \(x=-\frac34\).

sections.title: What if the other side can be negative?
sections.label: Check the signed side
sections.intro: For \(|u(x)|=v(x)\), a root must satisfy \(v(x)\ge0\). If you split by the sign of \(u(x)\), keep only candidates on their chosen branch.

blocks.html: Two equivalent routes are available. Impose \(v(x)\ge0\), then solve \(u(x)=v(x)\) or \(u(x)=-v(x)\). Alternatively, split where \(u(x)=0\), then retain roots satisfying each branch and the original equation.
In the example below, a solution is an intersection of the V and the line. The dashed part of the line has negative height, so it cannot intersect the V there.

figure.alt: The graph of y equals the modulus of 2x minus 1 intersects y equals x plus 4 at (−1, 3) and (5, 9). The portion of the line to the left of x equals −4 is dashed because it has negative height.
figure.caption: The vertical guide marks \(x=-4\). Keep only candidates on or to the right of this guide.

blocks.title: Test each candidate
blocks.prompt: Solve \(|x-1|=2x-3\). Give the complete real solution set.
blocks.hint: First require \(2x-3\ge0\). On that domain, \(x-1\) is already positive.
blocks.solution: The right-hand side requires \(x\ge\frac32\). Hence \(x-1=2x-3\), which gives \(x=2\). It satisfies the original equation.

retry.feedback: The candidate \(\frac43\) makes the right-hand side negative.
\(\frac43\) makes the right-hand side negative. Solve on \(x\ge\frac32\).

blocks.title: Recognise an empty solution set
blocks.hint: Check whether a distance can be negative.
blocks.solution: Every value of \(|x+2|\) is non-negative, so the solution set is empty.

blocks.html: Substitute candidate roots into the given equation when you have used a sign condition or squared a signed expression.
If the right side can be negative, establish its allowed region first. Both signed equations can still give a root when the right side is non-negative at each root.

blocks.title: Test both candidate roots
blocks.hint: The right side must be at least zero. Solve both signed cases on that region.
blocks.solution: The signed equations give \(x=3\) and \(x=-\frac53\). Both satisfy \(x\ge-4\), so include both.

sections.title: Can a whole interval satisfy a modulus equation?
sections.label: Recognise a whole branch
sections.intro: When solving branch by branch you may reach an identity. Then every point in that branch that meets the original restrictions is a solution.

blocks.html: For any real \(u\), the equation \(|u|=u\) means \(u\ge0\), and \(|u|=-u\) means \(u\le0\). Include \(u=0\).

blocks.title: Find the whole matching branch
blocks.hint: The modulus equals the negative of its input when the input is non-positive.
blocks.solution: The equation is equivalent to \(3x+9\le0\), or \(x\le-3\).

examples.title: Split into two signed values
examples.question: Solve \(|3x-5|=7\).
solution: Because the right side is positive, \(3x-5=7\) or \(3x-5=-7\).
\[3x-5=7\Longrightarrow x=4,\qquad 3x-5=-7\Longrightarrow x=-\frac23.\]
Both inner values have modulus \(7\). The complete answer is \(x=-\frac23\) or \(x=4\).

examples.title: Equal magnitudes do not force equal signs
examples.question: Solve \(|3x+4|=|2x-6|\).
solution: Equate the two expressions or equate one expression to the opposite of the other.
From \(3x+4=-(2x-6)\), obtain \(5x=2\), so \(x=\frac25\). Both cases give equal moduli.

examples.title: Keep the sign constraint
examples.question: Solve \(|2x-1|=x+4\).
solution: The right side must be non-negative, so \(x\ge-4\).
Both values satisfy \(x\ge-4\). The original sides are both \(9\) at \(x=5\), and both \(3\) at \(x=-1\).

examples.title: Find the only root at height zero
examples.question: Solve \(|4x+3|=0\).
solution: The inside must vanish, so \(4x+3=0\).
The solution set is \(\left\{-\frac34\right\}\).

examples.title: Handle an impossible signed case
examples.question: Solve \(|3x+8|=|3x-4|\).
solution: The equal-sign equation gives \(3x+8=3x-4\), which would require \(8=-4\).
The opposite-sign equation is \(3x+8=-3x+4\), giving \(x=-\frac23\).

examples.title: Retain both candidates after testing
examples.question: Solve \(|3x-2|=x+6\).
solution: The right side requires \(x\ge-6\). The two possible equations are \(3x-2=x+6\) and \(3x-2=-(x+6)\).
The candidates are \(x=4\) and \(x=-1\). Their respective right-side values are \(10\) and \(5\), so both are solutions.

examples.title: Find where the graphs share a ray
examples.question: Solve \(|2x-6|=2x-6\).
solution: The equation holds when the inner expression is non-negative. Therefore solve \(2x-6\ge0\).
The solution set is \(x\ge3\). The boundary value makes both sides zero.

glossary.definition: A possible root found during the algebra, before checking restrictions.
Two conditions that are true for exactly the same inputs.
An equation obtained by choosing the positive or negative value of the inside expression.
A candidate from a transformed equation that fails the original equation or one of its sign restrictions.
A statement that is true for every input in the region under consideration.
A region where a particular signed formula for the modulus is valid.

revision.body:
Equal to a constant

\(|u|=c\) has cases \(u=c\) and \(u=-c\) for \(c>0\). For \(c=0\) use \(u=0\); for \(c<0\) there are no real solutions.

Equal moduli

\(|u|=|v|\iff u=v\) or \(u=-v\). If you square these non-negative sides, the difference of squares gives the same cases.

A signed expression on one side

Keep \(v(x)\ge0\) before solving \(|u(x)|=v(x)\). For \(|2x-1|=x+4\), require \(x\ge-4\). Equating \(2x-1\) to \(x+4\) or \(-(x+4)\) gives \(x=5\) or \(x=-1\), and both pass the check.

Finish with a set

List each valid real solution once. Give exact fractions if they are required.

Recognise identical branches

\(|u|=u\) holds for \(u\ge0\) and \(|u|=-u\) holds for \(u\le0\). The solution may be an interval rather than isolated roots.
revision.checks:
• Write both signed cases.
  • Keep the original sign and domain restrictions.
  • Check all roots, then give their complete set.
revision.examTip: Squaring when one side may be negative can create extra candidates. Explain why you accept or discard each candidate.

extraPractice.title: Give both roots at a positive height
extraPractice.hint: Set the inner expression equal to positive seven and negative seven.

extraPractice.title: Compare two moduli
extraPractice.hint: The two inner expressions must be equal or be negatives of one another.
extraPractice.solution: The equal case \(2x+1=x-8\) gives \(x=-9\). The opposite case \(2x+1=-x+8\) gives \(x=\frac73\).

extraPractice.title: Check for inadmissible roots
extraPractice.hint: First find where the right side is non-negative. On that region, decide the sign of the inner expression.
extraPractice.solution: The right side requires \(x\ge\frac52\). There \(4x-3>0\), and the only linear candidate \(x=-1\) lies outside the allowed region. There are no solutions.

orig_9709_p3_alg_modulus_inequalities.description: Solve linear modulus inequalities using distance bands, difference of squares and signed branch restrictions.

sections.title: When do the solutions lie between two endpoints?
sections.label: Solve an inside band
sections.intro: \(|x-a|\) measures the distance from \(a\). A distance below a positive bound puts \(x\) inside an interval.

blocks.html:
\[|u|<c\iff -c<u<c\quad(c>0).\]

For \(\le\), include both endpoints by replacing both strict comparisons with \(\le\). If the bound is zero or negative, use \(|u|\ge0\) directly.
Equality holds at \(x=-4\) and \(x=3\). The strict comparison excludes them.

figure.alt: Number line showing the open interval from negative four to three. Both endpoints are open.
figure.caption: The interval \((-4,3)\) leaves out both endpoints.

blocks.title: Solve a two-sided inequality
blocks.hint: Write \(-5\le4x-3\le5\), then apply each operation to all three parts.
blocks.solution: Add \(3\) and divide by \(4\), giving \(-\frac12\le x\le2\).

retry.feedback: The original inequality is inclusive. Both boundary values satisfy it.

blocks.html: If the coefficient of \(x\) inside the modulus is negative, each comparison reverses when you divide by it. Put the endpoint values in increasing order at the end.

blocks.title: Find both inclusive endpoints
blocks.hint: Convert to a double inequality and reverse its signs when you divide by negative three.
blocks.solution: \(-4\le7-3x\le4\) gives \(-11\le-3x\le-3\). Thus \(1\le x\le\frac{11}3\).

sections.title: When do the solutions lie on two rays?
sections.label: Solve an outside band
sections.intro: A distance greater than a positive bound puts the variable outside the band.

blocks.html:
\[|u|>c\iff u<-c\ \text{or}\ u>c\quad(c>0).\]

For \(\ge\), keep the endpoints. Join the two conditions with “or”. At \(c=0\), \(|u|\ge0\) holds everywhere; \(|u|>0\) excludes exactly the zeros of \(u\).
The boundary inputs for \(|x+2|>4\) are \(-6\) and \(2\). Test the centre \(x=-2\). Its distance is zero, so the interval between the boundaries is excluded.

figure.alt: Number line for x less than negative six or x greater than two. Both endpoints are open. The centre negative two lies in the unshaded interval.
figure.caption: The two shaded rays continue outwards. The hollow endpoints give equality and are excluded.

blocks.title: Give both exterior rays
blocks.hint: Solve \(3x-6\le-9\) and \(3x-6\ge9\) separately.
blocks.solution: From the first branch \(x\le-1\). From the second \(x\ge5\). The solution is \(x\le-1\) or \(x\ge5\).

retry.feedback: The inequality requires at least the stated distance. Use the two exterior rays.
Include the ray to the left of the lower bound too.

sections.title: When can I square both sides safely?
sections.label: Compare two moduli
sections.intro: If both sides are moduli, they are non-negative. Squaring is increasing on non-negative numbers.

blocks.html: Turn the comparison into one about \(u^2-v^2=(u-v)(u+v)\). Then use a sign chart or test an input in each region. The roots split the number line into sign regions; they are included only if the comparison allows equality.

blocks.title: Read a strict product sign
blocks.hint: Factor the difference of squares as \((2x-2)(4x)\). Where is that product positive?
blocks.solution: Squaring gives \(8x(x-1)>0\). It is positive for \(x<0\) or \(x>1\). The comparison is strict.

retry.feedback: The product is negative between its two roots.
Both roots are equality cases, so exclude them from this strict comparison.

blocks.html: With two moduli, use the difference of two squares to determine where the squared magnitudes compare. The factor with lower root does not decide the sign by itself.

blocks.title: Include both exterior branches
blocks.hint: The difference of the squares factors as \((2x-4)(4x+6)\).
blocks.solution: The factors have the same sign for \(x<-\frac32\) or \(x>2\). The strict comparison excludes both roots.

sections.title: What if the second expression can be negative?
sections.label: Keep each branch restriction
sections.intro: Separate the regions where the inner linear expression is positive or negative. Solve the resulting inequality in each region and intersect it with that region.

blocks.html: For \(|u|\le v\), require \(v\ge0\) and use \(-v\le u\le v\). For \(|u|>v\), every input with \(v<0\) already satisfies the comparison. Splitting the modulus instead works for either direction.

blocks.title: Solve a variable-bound comparison
blocks.hint: Require \(x+1\ge0\), then write \(-(x+1)\le2x-4\le x+1\).
blocks.solution: The two bounds give \(3x\ge3\) and \(x\le5\), so \(1\le x\le5\). This interval already satisfies \(x\ge-1\).

retry.feedback: The lower comparison gives \(x\ge1\); keep that bound as well.

blocks.html: Squaring a comparison when the right-hand side is negative does not preserve the original inequality.

sections.title: What if the bound is zero or negative?
sections.label: Check non-positive bounds
sections.intro: A modulus is always non-negative. Compare that fact with the bound before trying to create a band or exterior rays.

blocks.html:
ComparisonWhen it holds
\(|u|<0\)Never
\(|u|\le0\)\(u=0\)
\(|u|>0\)\(u\ne0\)
\(|u|\ge0\)For every real value of the inside expression

blocks.title: Identify when an inequality is always true
blocks.hint: A modulus is non-negative for every real input, including where it is zero.
blocks.solution: Every real value of \(x\) satisfies the comparison. The solution set is \(\mathbb{R}\).

examples.title: An open distance band
examples.question: Solve \(|2x+1|<7\).
solution: Subtract \(1\) and divide by \(2\) throughout: \(-4<x<3\).
Neither endpoint is included. At each endpoint the original modulus equals the bound.

examples.title: Two exterior rays
examples.question: Solve \(|x+2|>4\).
solution: The inside expression must be below \(-4\) or above \(4\).
The result is \(x<-6\) or \(x>2\).

examples.title: Compare magnitudes by a product sign
examples.question: Solve \(|2x+1|\le|x-2|\).
solution: Both sides are non-negative, so square and subtract: \((2x+1)^2-(x-2)^2\le0\).
Factor to obtain \((x+3)(3x-1)\le0\), with zeros at \(-3\) and \(\frac13\).
The product is negative between its zeros and zero at either endpoint. Thus \(-3\le x\le\frac13\).

examples.title: Solve signed comparisons branch by branch
examples.question: Solve \(|x-3|>2x+1\).
solution: For \(x<3\), replace the modulus by \(3-x\). Then \(3-x>2x+1\) gives \(x<\frac23\), which lies on this branch.
For \(x\ge3\), replace the modulus by \(x-3\). Then \(x-3>2x+1\) gives \(x<-4\), impossible on this branch.
Take the union of the retained branch sets. The solution is \(x<\frac23\).

examples.title: Keep the order after dividing by a negative number
examples.question: Solve \(|5-2x|<3\).
solution: Write \(-3<5-2x<3\) and subtract five throughout: \(-8<-2x<-2\).
Divide by negative two, reversing both comparisons. This gives \(4>x>1\), usually written \(1<x<4\).

examples.title: Identify the signs either side of two roots
examples.question: Solve \(|2x-3|\le|x+3|\).
solution: Both sides are non-negative, so square and subtract: \((2x-3)^2-(x+3)^2=(x-6)(3x)\).
The factors have opposite signs between \(0\) and \(6\). The original comparison permits equality, so the solution is \(0\le x\le6\).

examples.title: Exclude the one zero-distance input
examples.question: Solve \(|3x+6|>0\).
solution: The modulus can only fail to be positive when the inside is zero.
The only excluded input is \(x=-2\). The solution is \(x\ne-2\).

glossary.definition: An interval between two finite boundary values.
An interval extending indefinitely in one direction.
The condition on the input under which a chosen signed formula for the modulus applies.
An endpoint where the relation may become equality. A strict inequality omits such a point.
All inputs in at least one of the solved regions.
Only the inputs meeting every condition under consideration. Use it when enforcing a branch restriction.

revision.body:
Distance rules

For \(c>0\), \(|u|<c\) means \(-c<u<c\). In contrast, \(|u|>c\) means \(u<-c\) or \(u>c\). Include equality at both boundaries for non-strict comparisons.

Example: \(|2x+1|<7\) gives \(-7<2x+1<7\), so \(-4<x<3\).

Two moduli

Both sides are non-negative. Square, factor \(u^2-v^2=(u-v)(u+v)\) and test the sign in each region.

A signed side

Split where the inside expression changes sign. Solve each linear comparison, intersect with its branch and join the retained sets. For \(|u|\le v\), equivalently require \(v\ge0\) and \(-v\le u\le v\).

Boundary values

A strict comparison excludes equality. Dividing an inequality by a negative number reverses the sign.

Check the sign of a constant bound

\(|u|<0\) is impossible, \(|u|\le0\) holds at \(u=0\), and \(|u|>0\) excludes that zero case.
revision.checks:
• Find equality points, then test the centre or a point in each region.
  • Use open endpoints when equality is excluded.
  • Join separate rays with “or”.
revision.examTip: For a signed right-hand side, write branch restrictions next to the rearranged inequalities. Keep the intersection on each branch first.

extraPractice.title: Find the two strict rays
extraPractice.hint: A distance exceeding seven puts the inner expression outside the band from −7 to 7.

extraPractice.title: Solve a comparison against a signed line
extraPractice.hint: Require a non-negative right side and compare both signed versions of the inside to that right side.
extraPractice.solution: The comparisons \(2x-5\le2x+1\) and \(-2x+5\le2x+1\) hold together exactly when \(x\ge1\). This also meets the sign condition.

extraPractice.title: Use the sign before splitting
extraPractice.hint: Check the least possible value of the modulus.
extraPractice.solution: A modulus is at least zero, so it cannot be less than negative three. There are no solutions.

extraPractice.title: Keep a constant factor when squaring
extraPractice.hint: Subtract the squares using the factored difference; one factor is a negative constant.
extraPractice.solution: The squared comparison reduces to \((-6)(6x+4)\le0\). Dividing by negative six reverses the sign, giving \(x\ge-\frac23\).

orig_9709_p3_alg_polynomial_division.description: Divide polynomials of degree up to four by a linear or quadratic polynomial and check the quotient and remainder.

sections.title: What must the quotient and remainder satisfy?
sections.label: Check the division identity
sections.intro: For a nonzero divisor \(D(x)\), write a polynomial \(P(x)\) as a multiple of \(D(x)\) plus a smaller remainder.

blocks.html:
\[P(x)=D(x)Q(x)+R(x).\]

Either \(R(x)=0\), or its degree is strictly below that of \(D(x)\). So dividing by a linear polynomial leaves a constant, while dividing by a quadratic can leave a linear expression.

blocks.title: Give both parts of a division
blocks.prompt: Divide \(x^3+3x^2+2x+7\) by \(x+2\). Give the quotient and the remainder.
blocks.hint: \((x+2)(x^2+x)=x^3+3x^2+2x\). Compare that product with the dividend.

blocks.html: A product-plus-remainder identity is a valid division result only when the remainder has lower degree than the divisor. If it still has a large enough leading term, another quotient term can be taken out.

blocks.title: Remove one more multiple of the divisor
blocks.prompt: Suppose \(P=(x^2-2)(x+4)+(3x^2+2x-1)\). Give the final quotient and remainder on division by \(x^2-2\).
blocks.hint: Take three times the divisor out of the displayed candidate remainder.
blocks.solution: Subtract \(3(x^2-2)\) from \(3x^2+2x-1\) to get \(2x+5\). The quotient grows from \(x+4\) to \(x+7\).

sections.title: How do I divide by a non-monic linear polynomial?
sections.label: Divide by a linear polynomial
sections.intro: At each step, divide the leading term of what remains by the leading term of the divisor. Multiply the whole divisor by that quotient term and subtract.

blocks.html: When the divisor is \(2x-1\), divide leading terms by \(2x\). Multiply by both terms of the divisor before subtracting.
Keep a column for each power, even if it has a zero coefficient. At every stage check that subtracting the multiple has cancelled the leading term.
Align like powers when subtracting and subtract every signed term of the product.

blocks.title: Account for a missing constant
blocks.hint: Start with quotient term \(x^2\), subtract \(3x^3+2x^2\), and keep a zero constant in the dividend.
blocks.solution: The next leading terms give quotient terms \(-x\) and \(2\). The result is \(3x^3-x^2+4x=(3x+2)(x^2-x+2)-4\).

blocks.html: The leading term division may give a fractional coefficient. Keep the fraction and multiply it by the whole divisor before subtracting.

blocks.title: Keep exact coefficients
blocks.prompt: Divide \(3x^2+2x-1\) by \(2x+1\). Give the quotient and remainder.
blocks.hint: The first quotient term is \(\frac32x\). Subtract its product before deciding the next term.
blocks.solution: The first subtraction gives \(\frac12x-1\) and the next quotient term is \(\frac14\). Hence \(Q=\frac32x+\frac14\) and \(R=-\frac54\).

sections.title: When do I stop dividing by a quadratic?
sections.label: Divide by a quadratic
sections.intro: Use the same leading-term rule. If a term is missing, leave a column for its power or write a zero coefficient.

blocks.html: Stop at degree less than \(2\). You may keep a remainder \(ax+b\). Check with \(DQ+R\).

blocks.title: Find a linear remainder
blocks.hint: The leading quotient terms are \(x^2\) and \(3x\). Stop when the degree left is at most \(1\).
blocks.solution: \((2x^2-1)(x^2+3x-2)=2x^4+6x^3-5x^2-3x+2\). The remaining \(4x+1\) has degree below \(2\).

sections.title: How do I check missing powers and exact division?
sections.label: Recognise exact division
sections.intro: A missing power in the dividend may come from cancellation between terms of \(D(x)Q(x)\). Check by multiplying back and adding the remainder. Exact division occurs when this remainder is zero.

sections.title: Why divide a rational expression first?
sections.label: Separate a polynomial and a proper fraction
sections.intro: Dividing a rational expression can separate it into a polynomial part and a proper fractional part. Keep the original excluded inputs when rewriting the result.

blocks.html: From \(P=DQ+R\), divide by \(D\) wherever \(D\ne0\) to obtain \(\frac PD=Q+\frac RD\). The smaller numerator \(R\) is ready for methods such as partial fractions.

blocks.title: Give the two parts and the exclusions
blocks.prompt: For \(\frac{2x^3-4x+3}{x^2-2}\), give quotient, remainder and every real input excluded by the original denominator.
blocks.hint: The product of \(2x\) with the divisor accounts for its two nonconstant terms. Find where the original denominator is zero.
blocks.solution: The product is \(2x^3-4x\), so \(Q=2x,\ R=3\). The excluded inputs are \(x=-\sqrt2\) and \(x=\sqrt2\).

examples.title: Verify a division without repeating long division
examples.question: A student claims that dividing \(x^3+2x^2-3x+4\) by \(x+3\) gives quotient \(x^2-x\) and remainder \(4\). Check the claim.
solution: Adding the proposed remainder \(4\) gives the original polynomial.
The remainder is constant, so it has lower degree than the divisor. The claim is correct.

examples.title: Use a non-monic linear divisor
examples.question: Divide \(2x^3+3x^2-8x+8\) by \(2x-1\).
solution:
Divide the leading terms: \(\frac{2x^3}{2x}=x^2\). Then multiply by the whole divisor and subtract.

\[\begin{aligned} &(2x^3+3x^2-8x+8)\\ &\quad -(2x^3-x^2)\\ &\quad =4x^2-8x+8.\end{aligned}\]
The next quotient term is \(2x\). Subtract \(4x^2-2x\) to leave \(-6x+8\).
The last quotient term is \(-3\). Subtract \(-6x+3\) to leave \(5\).

examples.title: Divide a quartic by a quadratic
examples.question: Divide \(2x^4-x^3+7x^2+3x+2\) by \(x^2+2\).
solution: The leading quotient term is \(2x^2\). Subtract \(2x^4+4x^2\) to leave \(-x^3+3x^2+3x+2\).
The next quotient term is \(-x\). Subtract \(-x^3-2x\) to leave \(3x^2+5x+2\).
Subtract \(3(x^2+2)\), leaving \(5x-4\) of degree \(1\), so stop.
The quotient is \(2x^2-x+3\) and the remainder is \(5x-4\).

examples.title: See missing powers cancel
examples.question: Divide \(x^4+x\) by \(x^2-1\).
solution: Write the dividend as \(x^4+0x^3+0x^2+x+0\). Use \(x^2\) as the first quotient term.
Subtract \(x^4-x^2\) to leave \(x^2+x\). The second quotient term is \(1\).
Subtract \(x^2-1\) to obtain \(R(x)=x+1\). Thus \(Q(x)=x^2+1\).
Check: \((x^2-1)(x^2+1)=x^4-1\). Adding the remainder \(x+1\) gives \(x^4+x\) as required.

examples.title: Repair a remainder with degree too high
examples.question: The division of \(P=x^3+4x^2+2x+1\) by \(D=x^2+x\) has reached \(P=D(x+1)+(2x^2+x+1)\). Finish the division.
solution: The candidate remainder still has degree two. Subtract \(2D=2x^2+2x\) from it.
The new remainder is \(-x+1\). Add two to the previous quotient, giving \(Q=x+3\) and \(R=-x+1\).

examples.title: Divide by a linear divisor with a fractional quotient
examples.question: Divide \(x^2+2x+3\) by \(2x-1\).
solution: The first quotient term is \(\frac x2\). Multiplying by \(2x-1\) gives \(x^2-\frac x2\). Subtract to leave \(\frac52x+3\).
The next quotient term is \(\frac54\). Its product with the divisor is \(\frac52x-\frac54\).
Subtract to obtain \(R=\frac{17}4\). The quotient is \(Q=\frac x2+\frac54\).

examples.title: Keep the restrictions when rewriting a fraction
examples.question: Rewrite \(\frac{x^3-x+2}{x^2-1}\) as a polynomial plus a proper fraction. State the excluded inputs.
solution: The first quotient term \(x\) gives product \(x(x^2-1)=x^3-x\). The remainder is \(2\).
Thus the form is \(x+\frac2{x^2-1}\), with the original exclusions \(x\ne-1,1\).

glossary.definition: The polynomial being divided.
The polynomial you divide by.
The polynomial multiplied by the divisor in the division identity.
The part left over, either zero or of lower degree than the divisor.
The term with the highest power of the variable and a non-zero coefficient.
A polynomial fraction with numerator degree lower than its denominator degree.
A value where the original denominator is zero. Rewriting the expression does not allow division by zero.

revision.body:
Use the identity

\(P=DQ+R\). The remainder is zero or has degree less than \(D\). A linear divisor leaves a constant; a quadratic divisor can leave \(ax+b\).

Repeat three operations

  • Divide the current leading term by the divisor's leading term.
  • Multiply the whole divisor by that quotient term.
  • Subtract the resulting polynomial and repeat only if the degree still allows another step.

Check a quartic division

\(x^4+x=(x^2-1)(x^2+1)+(x+1)\). Here \(Q=x^2+1\) and \(R=x+1\). The \(x^2\) terms cancel in the product.

Non-monic divisors

For \(3x+2\), divide the leading term by \(3x\) first. For \(2x^2-1\), divide it by \(2x^2\).

Rewrite a rational expression

\(\frac PD=Q+\frac RD\) where \(D\ne0\) and the final remainder has degree lower than the divisor.
revision.checks:
• Divide the current leading term by the divisor’s leading term.
  • Multiply by the entire divisor and subtract every term.
  • Check that the degree drops. Reconstruct the dividend at the end.
revision.examTip: State the quotient and remainder separately, even when the remainder is zero.

extraPractice.title: Divide a cubic with a missing term
extraPractice.hint: Keep a zero coefficient for the missing squared term.
extraPractice.solution: Multiplying back gives \((x-2)(x^2+2x-1)+2=x^3-5x+4\). The remainder is constant as required.

extraPractice.title: Stop at a linear remainder
extraPractice.hint: For a quadratic divisor, subtract until the remaining degree is at most one.
extraPractice.solution: The quotient terms are \(2x^2\) then \(x\) then \(1\). Subtracting the product leaves \(-2x+3\).

extraPractice.title: Use fractional coefficients in quadratic division
extraPractice.hint: Start with \(\frac32x^2\). The next quotient term accounts for the remaining squared term.
extraPractice.solution: After subtracting the first product, the squared coefficient is \(-\frac{11}{2}\), so the next quotient term is \(-\frac{11}4\). The final subtraction leaves \(\frac{41}4\).

extraPractice.title: Check an exact division by multiplying back
extraPractice.hint: Take the leading quotient term \(2x^2\) and continue until no remainder is left.
extraPractice.solution: Multiplying \((3x+2)(2x^2-x+1)\) gives the complete dividend. Thus the quotient is \(2x^2-x+1\) and the remainder is zero.

orig_9709_p3_alg_factor_remainder.description: Use the factor and remainder theorems with monic and non-monic divisors, find missing coefficients and solve polynomial equations.

sections.title: Which value gives a linear remainder?
sections.label: Evaluate the linear remainder
sections.intro: If you only need the remainder on division by \(ax+b\), find the input where the divisor is zero.

blocks.html:
\[P(x)=(ax+b)Q(x)+r,\quad r=P\left(-\frac ba\right),\quad a\ne0.\]

Substitution makes the product vanish. The remaining constant \(r\) is the remainder, even when the coefficient of \(x\) is not \(1\).

Use a zero of a linear divisor for a remainder or a factor check. If the question also asks for the quotient, use polynomial division. For a quadratic divisor the remainder can be linear, so one evaluation alone cannot determine it in general.

blocks.title: Evaluate at the zero of the divisor
blocks.prompt: Find the remainder when \(4x^3-8x^2+2x+1\) is divided by \(2x-1\).
blocks.hint: Use \(x=\frac12\), which makes \(2x-1=0\).
blocks.solution: The remainder is \(4\left(\frac12\right)^3-8\left(\frac12\right)^2+2\left(\frac12\right)+1=\frac12\).

blocks.html: For \(ax+b\), substitute \(-\frac ba\). Substituting \(-b\) is valid here only if \(a=1\) or \(b=0\).
The remainder on division by a non-monic linear divisor is still a constant. Its value comes from evaluating the dividend at the zero of that divisor.

blocks.title: Evaluate the dividend at the divisor's zero
blocks.prompt: Find the remainder when \(3x^3+2x-6\) is divided by \(3x-2\).
blocks.hint: The input is two thirds, not two.
blocks.solution: The value is \(3\left(\frac23\right)^3+2\left(\frac23\right)-6=\frac89+\frac43-6=-\frac{34}9\).

sections.title: How do factor and remainder conditions determine coefficients?
sections.label: Turn statements into equations
sections.intro: \(ax+b\) is a factor exactly when \(P\left(-\frac ba\right)=0\). A nonzero specified remainder gives a different evaluation equation.

blocks.html: Write one equation for each condition. Solve together, then check by substitution at both inputs.

blocks.title: Use both conditions
blocks.prompt: Let \(P(x)=x^3+ax^2+bx-8\). Given that \(x+1\) is a factor and division by \(x-2\) leaves remainder \(-6\), find \(a\) and \(b\).
blocks.hint: The equations come from \(P(-1)=0\) and \(P(2)=-6\).

blocks.html: Two pieces of information about linear divisions can give two independent equations. Use a zero value for a factor condition and the stated nonzero value for a remainder condition.

blocks.title: Use the correct evaluation at each root
blocks.prompt: Let \(P(x)=x^3+ax^2+bx-1\). The polynomial has factor \(x-1\) and remainder \(-21\) on division by \(x+2\). Find \(a,b\).
blocks.hint: Use the two values \(P(1)=0\) and \(P(-2)=-21\).
blocks.solution: These give \(a+b=0\) and \(4a-2b=-12\). Substituting \(b=-a\) yields \(a=-2,\ b=2\).

sections.title: How does a known factor help solve a cubic?
sections.label: Find every real root
sections.intro: Find or verify a linear factor, divide by it, and then solve the remaining factor. Keep the root from the first factor too.

blocks.html: If \(P\left(\frac32\right)=0\), both \(x-\frac32\) and \(2x-3\) are factors. The corresponding quotients have different coefficients, but the complete real root set is the same.

blocks.title: Keep every factor's root
blocks.prompt: \(2x-1\) is a factor of \(2x^3+x^2-13x+6\). Find all real roots of \(2x^3+x^2-13x+6=0\).
blocks.hint: Divide by \(2x-1\). The quotient \(x^2+x-6\) factorises into two linear terms.
blocks.solution: \(2x^3+x^2-13x+6=(2x-1)(x+3)(x-2)\), so the complete set is \(\left\{-3,\frac12,2\right\}\).

retry.feedback: Include the zero of the original divisor \(2x-1\).

blocks.html: A proposed factor is confirmed by one zero evaluation. To solve the whole equation, use the quotient too.
A factor may appear a second time in the quotient. In a set of solutions list that input once. When asked for multiplicity, count its occurrences as a factor separately.

figure.alt: The cubic crosses the horizontal axis at minus two and touches it at three.
figure.caption: The factors of \(P(x)=(x-3)^2(x+2)\) show a crossing at \(x=-2\) and contact without crossing at \(x=3\).

blocks.title: List each root once and count the repetition
blocks.prompt: Given factor \(x-1\), solve \(x^3+x^2-5x+3=0\). Give all distinct roots and the multiplicity of the root one.
blocks.hint: After dividing by the known factor, factorise the quadratic quotient.
blocks.solution: The quotient is \(x^2+2x-3=(x-1)(x+3)\). The roots are \(-3\) and \(1\), with multiplicity two at one.

sections.title: Can two evaluations determine a linear remainder?
sections.label: Use the two zeros of a quadratic divisor
sections.intro: Dividing by a quadratic produces a remainder of degree at most one. If the divisor has two distinct real zeros, the dividend and remainder agree at both of them.

blocks.html: For \(P=DQ+R\), at a zero \(r\) of \(D\) we have \(P(r)=R(r)\). Two distinct values of \(r\) determine the at-most-linear \(R(x)\).

blocks.title: Recover the remainder from two inputs
blocks.prompt: Find the remainder on division of \(P(x)=x^3+3x^2-x-13\) by \(x^2+x-6\).
blocks.hint: The divisor's zeros are two and negative three. At both inputs set a linear remainder equal to the dividend.

examples.title: Find a remainder without long division
examples.question: Find the remainder on dividing \(P(x)=2x^3-3x^2+4x+2\) by \(2x+1\).
solution: The divisor vanishes at \(x=-\frac12\). The remainder equals \(P\left(-\frac12\right)\).
\[P\left(-\frac12\right)=-\frac14-\frac34-2+2=-1.\]
The remainder is \(-1\), so \(2x+1\) is not a factor.

examples.title: Find two coefficients from two evaluations
examples.question: Let \(P(x)=x^3+ax^2+bx+6\). The factor \(x-1\) is given, and the remainder on division by \(x+2\) is \(12\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
solution: Add the equations to obtain \(3a=0\). Therefore \(a=0\), \(b=-7\). Check: \(1-7+6=0\) and \(-8+14+6=12\).

examples.title: Verify a factor and solve the cubic
examples.question: Verify that \(2x-3\) is a factor of \(P(x)=2x^3-9x^2+x+12\), then solve \(P(x)=0\).
solution: Evaluate at \(x=\frac32\): \(P\left(\frac32\right)=\frac{27}{4}-\frac{81}{4}+\frac32+12=0\). Hence \(2x-3\) is a factor.
Dividing by \(2x-3\) gives \(x^2-3x-4=(x+1)(x-4)\).

examples.title: Evaluate at a negative fractional root
examples.question: Find the remainder when \(2x^3-x^2+4x-5\) is divided by \(2x+1\).
solution: The divisor is zero at \(x=-\frac12\). Evaluate the dividend at that input.
The four terms give \(-\frac14-\frac14-2-5=-\frac{15}2\). This value is the constant remainder.

examples.title: Solve a factor condition and a remainder condition together
examples.question: Let \(P(x)=x^3+ax^2+bx+4\). The polynomial has factor \(x+1\) and remainder \(18\) on division by \(x-2\). Find \(a,b\).
solution: Add the equations to get \(3a=0\). Hence \(a=0,\ b=3\).

examples.title: Recognise a repeated factor in a cubic
examples.question: Given that \(x-3\) is a factor of \(x^3-4x^2-3x+18\), solve the cubic equation and state the multiplicity of the root three.
solution: Division by \(x-3\) gives \(x^2-x-6=(x-3)(x+2)\).
The factorisation is \((x-3)^2(x+2)\). The distinct roots are \(-2\) and \(3\), and three is a root of multiplicity two.

examples.title: Test a quadratic factor by two evaluations
examples.question: Show that \(x^2-x-2\) is a factor of \(P(x)=x^4-x^3-7x^2+5x+10\).
solution: Factor the divisor as \((x-2)(x+1)\). Direct substitution gives \(P(2)=0\) and \(P(-1)=0\).
The remainder has degree at most one and vanishes at two distinct inputs. It is the zero polynomial, so the quadratic divisor is a factor.

glossary.definition: \(ax+b\) is a factor of \(P(x)\) exactly when \(P\left(-\frac ba\right)=0\), for \(a\ne0\).
The constant remainder on division by \(ax+b\) is \(P\left(-\frac ba\right)\), for \(a\ne0\).
A value of the input where the polynomial equals zero.
The number of times the matching linear factor occurs in a factorisation.
Finding the value of a polynomial by substituting a stated input.
The at-most-first-degree expression left after division by a quadratic.

revision.body:
Evaluate at the divisor's zero

On division by \(ax+b\), \(r=P\left(-\frac ba\right)\). A remainder of zero confirms that \(ax+b\) is a factor.

Translate the condition

\(x-1\) is a factor means \(P(1)=0\). Remainder \(12\) for \(x+2\) means \(P(-2)=12\). Both statements can give equations for unknown coefficients.

Solve a polynomial completely

From \(2x^3-9x^2+x+12=(2x-3)(x+1)(x-4)\), the real roots are \(-1\), \(\frac32\) and \(4\). Include the root of the divisor as well as those of its quotient.

Quadratic divisors

For two distinct divisor zeros, use the two dividend values to find the coefficients of an at-most-linear remainder.
revision.checks:
• Check the sign and scale of the input you substitute.
  • For several conditions, check each evaluation after solving.
  • Factorise the quotient before writing your complete root set.
revision.examTip: A zero evaluation proves divisibility by the corresponding linear factor. To solve the polynomial equation, use the quotient to find the remaining roots.

extraPractice.title: Use a fractional evaluation point
extraPractice.prompt: Find the remainder on division of \(4x^2-3x+2\) by \(2x+3\).

extraPractice.title: Use a non-monic factor to find a coefficient
extraPractice.prompt: Given that \(2x-3\) is a factor of \(2x^2+ax-3\), find \(a\).
extraPractice.hint: The root is three halves. The polynomial must be zero there.

extraPractice.title: Find all the roots after removing a factor
extraPractice.prompt: The cubic \(2x^3+3x^2-11x-6\) has factor \(2x+1\). Give all real roots.
extraPractice.hint: Use the root of the given factor as well as the two roots of the quadratic quotient.
extraPractice.solution: The quotient is \(x^2+x-6=(x+3)(x-2)\). Together with the divisor zero this gives roots \(-3,-\frac12,2\).

extraPractice.title: Find a linear remainder by evaluation
extraPractice.prompt: Find the remainder when \(x^3-2x^2-3x+11\) is divided by \(x^2+x-2\).
extraPractice.hint: Use the divisor's zeros one and negative two to give two values of the remainder.
extraPractice.solution: The values are \(R(1)=7\) and \(R(-2)=1\). Solving for the coefficients gives \(R(x)=2x+5\).
